routes.description: Establish that contingent existence, religious experience, or moral obligation provides a defensible inference to an objective transcendent ground identifiable with God.
routes.successCriteria: At least one affirmative line must connect the relevant experience or fact to a necessary, objective, and non-arbitrary divine ground while answering the principal non-theistic alternative.

motionBridge.description: Show that at least one of the three proposed domains warrants affirming God's existence rather than merely describing human thought or feeling.

centralBridges.description: Connect experienced contingent beings and their totality to an external sufficient reason that does not itself require a further explanation.
Show that the character of religious experience is better explained by an objective transcendent cause than by a wholly subjective account.
Connect objective moral obligation and the authority of moral law to a transcendent ground of value that is neither arbitrary nor socially contingent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish an experiential inference to a necessary being from an a priori attempt to define that being into existence.
Explain how moral disagreement and culturally variable precepts remain open to criticism by reference to an objective ideal order.

routes.description: Show that the contingency, religious-experience, and moral-obligation arguments do not require God because their key inferences are invalid, underdetermined, or matched by non-theistic explanations.
routes.successCriteria: Prevent each affirmative line from reaching its divine conclusion by challenging its central inference or supplying an adequate account that does not presuppose a transcendent being.

motionBridge.description: Show that none of the proposed domains supplies sufficient grounds for moving from observed experience or practice to God's existence.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the application of necessity to beings and the inference from explanations of particular contingent things to an explanation of their totality.
Show that private experiences and their beneficial effects cannot discriminate an external divine object from subjective or incompatible interpretations.
Account for moral discrimination and obligation through feeling, custom, education, or imagined social disapproval without invoking divine authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require that claims about a being whose essence includes existence avoid treating existence as a predicate or reviving an ontological inference.
Use historical and cultural variation in perceived duties to test the asserted universality and absoluteness of moral law.

sections.title: Contingency and the meaning of necessary existence
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an empirically encountered contingent being can support a coherent modal inference to a being that cannot fail to exist.

sections.title: The totality of contingent beings and sufficient reason
sections.rationale: This issue tests the indispensable move from explanations within the world to an external explanation of the world or totality as such.

sections.title: Religious experience and an objective transcendent cause
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the distinctive character of mystical awareness supplies grounds for an objective divine reality rather than a subjective event.

sections.title: Competing reports and transformative effects
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether conviction, beneficial transformation, and experiential veracity can distinguish divine contact from incompatible or fictional objects.

sections.title: Moral feeling, objective value, and critical standards
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether moral distinctions require an objective standard and whether identifying goodness with a divine source establishes rather than assumes God.

sections.title: Moral obligation, variation, and its explanatory ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the authoritative sense of obligation requires a transcendent lawgiver or is adequately explained by historical customs, education, and social disapproval.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Because no contingent object contains the reason for its own existence, the totality of contingent objects requires a sufficient reason external to that totality.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is Copleston's announced, uninterrupted statement of his metaphysical argument from contingency.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly advances the contingency route by demanding an external sufficient reason for the totality of contingent objects.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely develops the principal affirmative inference assigned to this constructive class.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but the shift between reason, explanation, and existent being leaves one material term bridge compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated necessity exceeds the supplied defense because aggregation and the externality of the reason are asserted rather than established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move is intelligible but leaves substantial composition and sufficient-reason bridges unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It relies on a general metaphysical principle and supplies no independent defense of its application to the totality.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly contacts the indispensable central contingency bridge and nearly exhausts that tier's assigned issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own positive inference and does not materially interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly moves from contingent objects lacking internal reasons to an external existent reason for their totality.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions, so a necessary being is admissible only if denying that being's existence is self-contradictory.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell explicitly introduces this as his starting answer to Copleston's argument and develops it in one turn.

components.text: Whether the proposed external reason can coherently be a necessary being.
Whether the totality requires any external sufficient reason at all.

response.rationale: Russell contacts the necessary-being component by restricting necessity to analytic propositions, but does not yet answer the inference from totality to an external reason.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that reaches an important modal component while leaving the totality demand untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analytic standard is clear, though the claim that necessity applies only to propositions has a broad and insufficiently defended scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The restriction is forcefully stated and defined, but its exclusivity is broader than the brief logical account warrants.

charity.alternative: A necessary being may be inferred conditionally from experienced contingency rather than proved by an analytic existence proposition.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conditional inference still requires a defended modal bridge from contingency to necessary existence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analytic criterion is internally clear, but the exclusive restriction of necessity remains a material unsupported premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific semantic test is supplied, though no substantial defense is given for excluding de re or conditional necessity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally challenges the modal coherence of the contingency route, though not its totality inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: Russell treats necessary being chiefly through analyticity and does not fully accommodate the experiential conditional interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell explicitly confines significant necessity to analytic propositions and requires contradiction in denying the being's existence.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Although the existence of a contingent being must be learned from experience, once such a being is known to exist, the inference to a necessary being follows with necessity.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston states the conditional proposition, accepts Russell's terminology provisionally, and distinguishes its empirical premise.

components.text: Whether an empirical premise can support a necessary conditional inference without itself being analytic.

response.rationale: Copleston directly distinguishes the empirical discovery of a contingent being from the claimed necessity of the inference once that premise is known.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts Russell's analytic objection and supplies the intended empirical-versus-conditional distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The empirical premise and claimed necessary consequence are clearly distinguished, with the conditional scope made express.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional qualification is explicit, but the necessity of the consequence is asserted without the premise that would derive it.

charity.alternative: Russell's objection concerns whether any existential conclusion can be analytic, not whether the initial contingency premise is empirical.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston must still show why the empirical fact entails a necessary being rather than merely permitting that hypothesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is coherent, but the central bridge from one contingent being to a necessary being remains unstated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Experience supports the contingent premise only; it does not itself verify the claimed necessary consequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary modal-coherence bridge by separating empirical knowledge from an a priori proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes the empirical premise, while leaving Russell's strongest entailment challenge incompletely resolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls the existence of a contingent being empirical while claiming its consequence follows necessarily.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Defining a being whose essence involves existence revives the ontological argument, but existence is not a predicate and cannot be asserted analytically of a named subject.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell identifies the alleged ontological implication and then gives his logical account of meaningful existence claims.

components.text: Whether the claimed necessary being avoids an ontological inference that treats existence as a predicate.
Whether contingent totality requires an external sufficient reason.

response.rationale: Russell identifies the alleged inference as ontological and states the defeating consequence that existence cannot function as an analytic predicate of a named subject.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses a logical defect in the necessary-existence formulation, although it does not address the separate totality premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The predicate objection, named-versus-described distinction, and alleged ontological consequence are all expressly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical thesis is clearly articulated, though its application to every experiential modal inference is somewhat broader than shown.

charity.alternative: Copleston may infer a necessary being from experience and only subsequently characterize its essence, avoiding definition into existence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The subsequent characterization still must not use existence as an ordinary predicate or substitute for the missing inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection gives a consistent logical account and a clear defeating consequence, with only a bounded application gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The named-versus-described analysis specifically supports the objection, though rival quantificational treatments are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary existence-analysis bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Russell identifies a serious logical risk but somewhat compresses the distinction between an experiential inference and an ontological proof.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell expressly links essence-involving-existence to the ontological argument and denies that existence is a predicate.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: God is inferred from experience rather than known a priori, and divine essence and existence must be identical because otherwise God's existence would require a sufficient reason beyond God.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston expressly distinguishes his experiential inference from an argument based solely on an intuition of God's essence.

components.text: Whether Copleston's argument defines God into existence or begins from experience.
Whether necessary existence must be known through an analytic proposition.

response.rationale: Copleston directly denies a priori knowledge and locates the inference in experience, then explains why he identifies divine essence and existence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It substantially contacts both earlier logical objections, though the sufficient-reason step remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The experiential qualification is explicit, but essence, existence, identity, and sufficient reason are connected with a compressed conceptual transition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply properly limits a priori knowledge, but the asserted identity of essence and existence is not established by the brief regress claim.

charity.alternative: Russell's objection may target the later characterization of divine existence even if the initial inference begins empirically.
charity.decisiveQualification: An empirical starting point does not by itself show that essence and existence are identical.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experiential distinction is coherent, while the inference from avoiding a further reason to essence-existence identity remains material and implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Experience is invoked as the starting basis, but neither the inferred being nor the identity claim receives independent verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary modal-coherence requirement and distinguishes its method from an a priori proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: Copleston fairly answers the a priori reading but does not fully resolve the strongest predicate-based objection to the later identity claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston states that knowledge begins through experience and argues that otherwise a sufficient reason would lie beyond God.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Although observation supports causal explanations for particular things, it supplies no reason to suppose that the totality of particular things has any cause whatsoever.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell grants causal explanation for a particular object and immediately rejects extending that concept to the totality.

components.text: Whether causal explanation of particulars licenses a cause or sufficient reason for their totality.
Whether experience of contingency entails a necessary being.
Whether the inferred being has identical essence and existence.

response.rationale: Russell expressly diagnoses the extension from observed particular causes to a cause of the whole as unwarranted and denies the resulting totality demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly attacks the decisive totality inference and states why observation of particulars does not support it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clear, though causal explanation and sufficient reason are treated together without distinguishing their potentially different scopes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Russell claims absence of reason rather than impossibility, fitting the limited observational warrant he invokes.

charity.alternative: Copleston seeks a sufficient reason rather than an observed temporal cause for the totality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell must distinguish those notions, although the extrapolation beyond particulars still requires defense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The anti-extrapolation inference is coherent, with one bounded ambiguity between cause and sufficient reason.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It grounds causal concepts in observation of particulars but does not fully compare the metaphysical sufficient-reason alternative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable central inference from particular explanations to explanation of the totality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection captures the extrapolation problem but partly weakens the argument by translating sufficient reason into cause.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell grants causal explanation of particulars but expressly finds no reason to extend causation to all particular objects.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The basic mystical awareness of a loving, transcendent, nonconceptual reality is more adequately explained by an objective cause than as an experience produced wholly within the subject.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston announces the religious-experience topic, defines the relevant experience, and states his explanatory inference.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the religious-experience route by describing mystical awareness and inferring that a wholly subjective account is inadequate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely presents the central affirmative explanatory claim for this constructive class.

precisionFindings.rationale: The described experience and subjective alternative are clear, but the scope of the claim across mystical experiences is not delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that subjective explanation cannot suffice is stronger than the phenomenological description alone warrants.

charity.alternative: The experience may irresistibly seem transcendent while being generated wholly within the subject.
charity.decisiveQualification: Phenomenal certainty during an experience does not independently establish an external object.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory conclusion is intelligible, but the bridge from phenomenology to an objective cause remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant rests on generalized experiential description without representative documentation or comparison with psychological alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central affirmative inference from mystical awareness to an objective transcendent cause.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mentions the subjective account but largely dismisses it without testing how internally generated experiences can share those features.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes a loving transcendent-seeming awareness and claims that it cannot be adequately explained wholly subjectively.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Private mystical reports do not establish God because equally convinced reports concern demons or Satan, which cannot all be accepted on the same testimonial basis.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell states his agnostic conclusion and compares mystical testimony with similarly confident reports of rejected supernatural beings.

components.text: Whether private mystical conviction discriminates God from incompatible reported objects.

response.rationale: Russell identifies testimonial parity with equally inward and confident Satan reports and states that the same basis cannot selectively establish God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the decisive discrimination problem and gives the defeating consequence for the experiential inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The parity comparison, its testimonial basis, and its limited consequence for an argument from reports are clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Russell claims that the reports do not supply a discriminating argument, a force matched to the counterexample.

charity.alternative: Copleston may rely on a common basic transcendent experience while treating divergent interpretations as secondary.
charity.decisiveQualification: The shared phenomenology still needs criteria that favor an objective divine cause over incompatible or subjective interpretations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity objection is explicit, consistent, and directly defeats an inference based solely on equally confident private reports.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific incompatible-report class supports the underdetermination claim, though prevalence and independence are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con bridge requiring discrimination between divine and incompatible subjective interpretations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The parity objection fairly reaches the testimonial problem, with only a minor omission concerning a possible common experiential core.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell compares inward reports of God with phenomenologically similar reports of Satan and denies selective evidential force.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: A profound and wholesome transformation caused by an experience is not evidence that the experience involved any reality outside the subject.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell appeals to his own transformative experiences and explicitly denies that their effects evidence an external object.

components.text: Whether profound beneficial transformation verifies a reality external to the experiencer.
Whether the phenomenology itself is better explained by an objective transcendent cause.

response.rationale: Russell expressly separates wholesome transformative effect from external-object verification, defeating that corroborative warrant while leaving the basic phenomenological inference unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer decisively contacts the transformation component but not the primary phenomenological explanation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between character change and external-object evidence is sharply and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The personal counterexample appropriately supports the limited claim that beneficial effects do not by themselves verify external reality.

charity.alternative: Transformation may corroborate an experience when combined with its distinctive phenomenology and other evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Transformation alone remains nondiscriminating because internally caused experiences can also transform character.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between pragmatic effect and ontological verification is explicit and logically complete for the targeted warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete personal counterexample supports the logical point, though the empirical range of transformative experiences is not surveyed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central religious-experience challenge by removing one proposed discriminator.

representationalCharity.rationale: Russell accurately isolates the limited evidential role at issue and preserves the qualification that the effect by itself is insufficient.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell cites profound wholesome experiences that involved no external object and denies that beneficial effect proves one.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: A morally beneficial response to a loved historical or fictional figure does not establish that the figure actually exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly develops Russell's skeptical counterexample and is followed by Copleston's explicit agreement and qualification.

components.text: Whether beneficial influence from a loved apparent object establishes that object's existence.
Whether mystical phenomenology independently warrants an objective cause.

response.rationale: Russell supplies a fictional or mistakenly believed historical figure whose beneficial influence persists without existence, defeating the transformation-to-existence inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The counterexample decisively contacts corroboration by beneficial effect but leaves the basic mystical phenomenology component untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterexample and its limited conclusion about influence failing to establish existence are recoverable and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample matches the limited negative conclusion and does not purport to disprove every possible experiential argument.

charity.alternative: Direct mystical acquaintance may differ epistemically from influence through a narrative or mistaken historical belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy defeats beneficial transformation alone, not necessarily every feature of alleged direct acquaintance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample validly shows that beneficial influence does not entail the existence of its represented object.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete possible case adequately supports the logical counterexample, though its analogy to direct experience has a bounded gap.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central underdetermination bridge by defeating beneficial transformation as a discriminator.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply uses a fair counterexample for transformative effects while leaving a bounded difference between narrative influence and mystical experience.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell describes morally beneficial influence by a nonexistent figure and separates that influence from the figure's existence.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Identifying love of genuine goodness with love of God risks merely defining God as goodness rather than independently establishing God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell frames the position as a direct question to Copleston, whose immediately following answer accepts that further argument is required.

components.text: Whether mystical awareness is better explained by an objective transcendent cause.

response.rationale: The question raises a new, issue-bearing concern about defining God as goodness, but it does not contact the decisive mystical-experience demand in any legal earlier target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a relevant nonanswer within the available target topology because its actual moral claim has no earlier opposing locked target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Russell clearly frames the suspected definitional equivalence and explicitly marks the need for further argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interrogative and risk-based framing exactly match the preliminary warrant available in the exchange.

charity.alternative: Goodness may reflect or proceed from God without being definitionally identical to God.
charity.decisiveQualification: That theological relation still requires independent support for God's existence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The circularity diagnosis is coherent and correctly identifies that definitional substitution would not independently establish existence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The wording of the asserted identification supplies a specific basis, while the question appropriately awaits clarification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: No exact route burden is contacted because the move tests a definitional issue outside the available adopted burden bridges.

representationalCharity.rationale: Russell poses the circularity concern as a question and leaves room for Copleston to distinguish reflection from identity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell asks whether God has merely been defined as the good and explicitly says that such an identification requires argument.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Goodness is not identical with God in a pantheistic sense, but what is truly good reflects and proceeds from God, though this interpretation depends on independently recognizing God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer explicitly rejects pantheism, states Copleston's own theological view, and concedes the dependence of that interpretation on God's existence.

components.text: Whether Copleston is merely defining God as the sum or system of goodness.

response.rationale: Copleston directly denies pantheistic identity, substitutes a reflects-and-proceeds relation, and concedes that this interpretation depends on prior recognition of God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the definitional challenge and provides both the distinction and its limiting concession.

precisionFindings.rationale: The denial of identity, the proposed dependence relation, and the concession about prior recognition are all explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move carefully presents a theological interpretation and expressly concedes that it cannot independently establish God.

charity.alternative: Russell's concern is that any connection between goodness and God may remain circular without independent establishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting identity avoids simple definition, but the reflects-and-proceeds claim still presupposes God's existence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between identity and dependence is explicit and consistent, and the concession prevents an illicit existential inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual clarification is well supported by the stated view, though the divine-source relation itself receives no independent evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move clarifies a theological interpretation but expressly does not complete any adopted existence-establishment bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Copleston accurately addresses the strongest circularity concern and expressly acknowledges the decisive remaining dependence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston denies that God is the sum of goodness and concedes that the proposed interpretation presupposes recognizing God.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Moral distinctions need no external theological justification because good and bad can be discriminated through feeling, much as colors are distinguished through perception.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell answers Copleston's direct question in the first person and sustains the perceptual analogy until Copleston introduces a concrete moral test case.

components.text: Whether goodness reflects and proceeds from an independently recognized divine source.

response.rationale: Russell supplies an issue-bearing non-theological account of moral discrimination, but it does not answer Copleston's immediately earlier dependence claim about goodness and God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a relevant nonanswer to the legal earlier target while strongly developing a separate moral issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: The feeling analogy is clear, but feeling shifts between a discriminating faculty and the apparent referent of moral predicates.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy supports possible discrimination without theology, but not yet the authority or correctness of moral judgments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy explains discrimination but leaves a material bridge from felt difference to moral correctness and obligation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The color analogy is illustrative rather than independently evidential and does not compare error, disagreement, or authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con morality bridge by proposing feeling as a non-theological account of discrimination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers Russell's positive analogy rather than a developed interpretation of an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell expressly says good and bad are distinguished by feeling, using visual color discrimination as his analogy.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Differences in felt response cannot by themselves settle whether a judgment is sound, because without an objective criterion beyond feeling there is no basis for condemning even atrocious conduct.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn continues Copleston's questioning of Russell's feeling theory and contrasts the commandant's behavior with exemplary religious conduct.

components.text: Whether feeling alone supplies a standard for condemning morally atrocious conduct.

response.rationale: Copleston identifies the absence of an objective criterion as the defect in the feeling account and states the consequence that condemnation loses rational basis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly contacts the decisive adequacy problem in Russell's feeling analogy and gives its defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional absence of an objective criterion and the resulting problem for condemnation are clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The challenge is forceful and pertinent, though feeling theories could potentially add intersubjective or natural standards.

charity.alternative: A feeling-based account may appeal to normal human capacities, shared responses, or corrected perception rather than bare individual preference.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such an account still must explain why normality supplies moral authority rather than mere prevalence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection consistently exposes the gap between subjective discrimination and justified condemnation, with one bounded alternative-account omission.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete atrocious-conduct test makes the normative gap specific, though it does not eliminate every objective naturalistic criterion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con morality bridge by challenging feeling as an adequate account of moral judgment.

representationalCharity.rationale: Copleston engages the colorblindness analogy and presses its strongest normative gap, with only a minor compression of possible natural standards.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston asks what objective basis remains for condemning atrocious conduct if moral judgment refers only to feeling.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The perception of values and consciousness of moral obligation are best explained by a transcendent ground of value and a non-arbitrary author of moral law.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston explicitly introduces moral obligation as an approach to God's existence and states the explanatory hypothesis in an uninterrupted turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly advances the moral-obligation route by proposing a transcendent, non-arbitrary ground for values and obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly states the principal affirmative explanatory hypothesis assigned to the constructive moral route.

precisionFindings.rationale: Values, obligation, transcendent ground, and non-arbitrary authorship are consistently stated, with the anti-arbitrariness qualification express.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The best-explanation claim lacks comparison with naturalistic accounts, despite explicitly excluding arbitrary authorship.

charity.alternative: Moral perception and obligation may arise from human feeling, social formation, or rational relations without a transcendent author.
charity.decisiveQualification: A divine hypothesis needs comparative explanatory advantage and a bridge from authority to a personal source.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The hypothesis is intelligible, but the inference from obligation to a transcendent author contains a material unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies the phenomena and a hypothesis but no representative evidence or serious comparison with rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge connecting moral obligation to a non-arbitrary transcendent ground.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move asserts superior explanation without substantially testing the principal non-theological alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston expressly calls a transcendent ground and non-arbitrary author the best explanation of value perception and obligation.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: There is no absolute moral law because perceived moral requirements change historically, with practices such as cannibalism once regarded as duties.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell explicitly rejects absoluteness and immediately supplies historical moral variation as his supporting example before Copleston answers.

components.text: Whether moral law is absolute given substantial historical change in perceived duties.

response.rationale: Russell directly rejects absoluteness and supplies cannibalism once treated as duty as evidence of historical moral variation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly contacts the asserted absoluteness component with a concrete historical counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The example is clear, but moral law shifts between objective law and historically perceived duty, while the universal claim is unqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Variation in belief supports fallibility or changing codes, but does not by itself establish that no absolute standard exists.

charity.alternative: An absolute moral standard may remain fixed while human beliefs about particular duties vary or err.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical variation tests epistemic access but does not logically refute an invariant objective standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from variable perceived duties to no absolute moral law contains a substantial belief-versus-truth equivocation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cannibalism is a specific example of variation, but one selective example cannot establish the universal metaphysical conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary moral-variation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Russell materially compresses the distinction between changing moral beliefs and change in the moral standard itself.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell cites changing moral requirements and the historical treatment of cannibalism as a duty to deny absoluteness.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The possibility of criticizing culturally accepted moral codes presupposes an objective ideal moral order whose obligatory character can be recognized and whose real foundation is God.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston rejects divine dictation of particular precepts, distinguishes their variable content from an objective standard, and concludes with God as foundation.

components.text: Whether changing accepted codes defeats an objective ideal moral order.
Whether moral criticism requires a standard beyond feeling and accepted practice.

response.rationale: Copleston distinguishes accepted codes from a criticizable ideal order and states that variation does not defeat the objective standard presupposed by criticism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the code-versus-standard conflation and also contacts the earlier feeling-account problem.

precisionFindings.rationale: Accepted code, objective standard, ideal order, obligatory character, and divine foundation are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The presupposition of an objective critical standard is plausible, but its identification with a real divine foundation is asserted too strongly.

charity.alternative: Moral criticism may use internal consistency, human flourishing, or revised social standards without a transcendent ideal order.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston must show why criticism requires mind-independent obligation and why that obligation requires God.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The code-versus-ideal distinction is coherent, while the final inference from objective criticism to God remains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The practice of moral criticism supports some standard, but not without further argument an objective divine foundation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary objective-criticism bridge at the top of that relevance tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes codes from standards but omits strong non-theistic accounts of critical standards.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston distinguishes variable accepted codes from an objective criticizable ideal order and identifies God as its foundation.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: The sense of moral obligation can be explained as imagined disapproval produced by customs, taboos, environment, and education rather than by a transcendent lawgiver.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell states a first-person explanatory account of the sense of ought, after which Copleston explicitly answers by distinguishing moral form from content.

components.text: Whether the sense of obligation requires a transcendent author rather than natural social formation.
Whether objective criticism and obligatory character require a divine foundation.

response.rationale: Russell directly supplies imagined disapproval, custom, taboo, environment, and education as an alternative explanation of the felt ought, but does not answer objective criticism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer reaches the decisive explanatory component while leaving the objective-authority component untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanandum, imagined-disapproval mechanism, and environmental sources are clearly and consistently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account plausibly explains a sense of ought, but it is presented as easier explanation without comparative evidence or normative analysis.

charity.alternative: Copleston distinguishes the psychological sense of obligation from the objective authority or validity of moral law.
charity.decisiveQualification: A causal genealogy of the feeling does not by itself explain or defeat any objective normative authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal account is coherent for felt obligation but leaves the material bridge from psychological origin to normative sufficiency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete social mechanisms are named, though their adequacy is asserted without representative evidence or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con morality bridge with a developed non-theological explanation of obligation.

representationalCharity.rationale: Russell offers a relevant psychological rival but materially underaddresses Copleston's distinction between felt origin and objective validity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell explains the sense of ought through imagined disapproval, customs, taboos, environment, and education.
